getting-started.title: 🚀 Getting started
getting-started.text: 🚀 Getting started The folders it needs The plugin is developed next to the projects it uses: go.mod replaces Go Simulator, Go Renderer and Go Scene Builder with the folders beside this one. Clone them side by side: go-renderer/ go-scene-builder/ go-simulator/ go-simulator-climate/ ← this repository A rules file The plugin needs one thing from your world: a relief, in Go Scene Builder's format ( relieve.json , with the heights in relieve.f32 next to it, in kilometres east and north). The rest is numbers in a rules file. This one, climate.yaml in the go-simulator folder, is the one the pictures in these pages were made with, on a made-up island: plugins: - name: climate command: [go, run, .] directory: ../go-simulator-climate stages: - name: year clock: {unit: month, from: 0, to: 12, step: 0.25, pace: 0.5} snapshots: [0] snapshot_fields: [temperature, precipitation, biome] rules: - rule: climate with: relief: relieve.json origin: [10, 7.5] cell: 0.1 temperature: {sea_level: 12, lapse: 6.5} rain: {wind_from: 270, background: 800, orographic: 1800} terrain: {river_area: 5, river_slope: 0.04} biomes: - {biome: snow, when: {temperature: {max: -2.5}}} - {biome: rock, when: {slope: {min: 0.6}}} - {biome: riverside, when: {river: true}} - {biome: coast, when: {coast: true}} - {biome: forest, when: {temperature: {max: 11}, precipitation: {min: 1000}}} - {biome: meadow, when: {precipitation: {min: 750}}} - {biome: steppe} regions: - {biome: old wood, ellipse: {centre: [5.2, 8.4], radii: [2.2, 1.6]}, ragged: 0.15, when: {height: {min: 150}}} - rule: seasons with: year_length: 12 warmest: 0.55 temperature: {sea_level: 12, lapse: 6.5, amplitude: 8} snow_at: 0 snow_blend: 150 foliage: - {at: 0.25, color: "#9cc35a", amount: 0.15} - {at: 0.5, color: "#5d7a3c", amount: 0} - {at: 0.8, color: "#c8752f", amount: 0.6} - {at: 0.95, color: "#7a6e5f", amount: 0.6} The plugin starts with go run from this repository, so it needs no installing. The stage is a year of months, a quarter of a month a step; pace is how many real seconds a step takes in the viewer. Every key is in Go Simulator's rules files , and every parameter of the two rules in the rules reference . Without a window cd ../go-simulator && go run ./cmd/simulate -rules climate.yaml -output results Go Simulator runs the year as fast as it can and saves, in results/ , the three fields as grids ( year 0 biome.json with year 0 biome.f32 next to it, and so on), and every event in events.jsonl , among them the biomes event with the name of every biome: {"data":{"names":["snow","rock","riverside","coast","forest","meadow","steppe","old wood"]},"name":"biomes","origin":"climate","stage":"","time":0} The flora plugin reads the fields from the world to grow vegetation. For Go Scene Builder , which colours the terrain and sows each biome's vegetation from a layer ( -layer biome=… ), add layer: biomes.json to the climate rule: it saves biomes.json and biomes.f32 next to the rules file, with the biome names as labels and in the relief's kilometres east and north, so the layer lines up with the relief whatever the origin (see the model ). In the viewer To see the island in 3D, Go Scene Builder builds a scene from the relief, coloured by the biomes, and Go Simulator's viewer shows it while the rules run: cd ../go-scene-builder go run ./cmd/build-scene -map empty.geojson -relief relieve.json -layer biome=biomes.json -style style.yaml -out island.glb cd ../go-simulator go run ./cmd/simulator -rules climate.yaml island.glb go run ./cmd/simulator -rules climate.yaml -advance 26 -capture summer.png island.glb The style gives every biome a colour under terrain.biomes (see Go Scene Builder's decoration ), and empty.geojson is a map with no features. -advance 26 steps the year 26 times before showing, to month 6.5. biomes.json is the layer the climate rule saves with layer: biomes.json . The snapshot's year 0 biome.json will not do as it is: it has no names, and its edges are the world's, which match the relief's only with origin: [0, 0] . The tests go vet ./... go test ./... The tests build a round island with a ridge running north to south and check that the ridge is as cold as its height says, that the slope facing the west wind is wetter than the other, that snow, sea and a region's biome land where they should, and that the seasons move the snow line and the foliage around the year. Others read the biome layer back with Go Scene Builder's own loader, with an origin away from zero, work the climate out on the world's ground and drainage and again when that ground rises, and check that every rule describes its contracts.

how-it-works.title: 🔍 How it works

sections.text: How the plugin fits Go Simulator
What happens at the start and every step

how-it-works.text: 🔍 How it works How the plugin fits Go Simulator Go Simulator is the host. It keeps the world (its entities, fields and environment) and moves the clock. The climate plugin is a separate program the host starts; they talk over standard input and output (Go Simulator's protocol ). At the start the plugin describes itself: its two rules, their parameters, what each one reads and what it writes. That description is also where the rules reference comes from. climate reads nothing from other plugins. It loads the relief named in its parameters and writes the fields temperature , precipitation and biome , and the biomes event with the name of every biome. seasons reads the environment and writes environment : the snow line ( snow ) and the foliage tint ( foliage_tint ). A plugin never touches the renderer: it reads its copy of the world and answers with changes (Go Simulator's writing plugins ). Fields use physical units and shapes world units, as Go Simulator's vocabulary lists. Other plugins read the fields from the world instead of working the climate out again. What happens at the start and every step At the start , climate works the climate out and publishes it. If a stage does not start it, the first step does instead. Later steps leave it as it is: the climate does not change with time yet. At the start and every step , seasons takes the share of the year the stage's time has reached ( time / year_length , around and around), works out the season's temperature at sea level, sea_level + amplitude × cos(2π × (share − warmest)) , and from it the height of the snow line, (that temperature − snow_at) / lapse km, never below sea level. The foliage tint is the foliage stops interpolated at the same share, from the last stop round to the first. Both work on any clock: a stage of months with year_length: 12 , or a real-time stage with year_length: 240 for a year every four minutes. How the pictures were made The pictures of the made-up island in these pages were drawn from the plugin's own answers. A small throwaway program, kept outside the repository, wrote a made-up relief (an island 20 km by 15 km, with a ridge in the east, a hill in the west and three valleys), ran the real plugin inside a Go Simulator host with the rules file in getting started , read back the three fields and the environment after every step of the year, and drew them: the maps, the cut across the island, the year of seasons and the chart of biomes. The map with the wind from the east and the one without the region are the same run with wind_from: 90 , or with no regions . Maps are PNG pictures in a light and a dark version; the charts are SVG with their own light and dark colours. The 3D pictures are Go Simulator's viewer: the same rules run with cmd/simulate , Go Scene Builder built a scene from the relief coloured by the biome snapshot, and the viewer captured a frame ( -capture ) at month 0.25 and month 6.5 ( -advance 1 , -advance 26 ), and at night ( -night ) for the dark version of the picture at the top of the README. The diagrams (how it fits, the model, the steps) were drawn by hand in the same style. The picture of the example island at the top of the climate model came with the repository and was kept as it was.

overview.title: Welcome to Go Climate Simulator 👋

sections.text: All the pages, in reading order

overview.text: Welcome to Go Climate Simulator 👋 The climate plugin gives a simulated world its weather : how warm, how wet, where it snows, and which landscape ( biome ) each place has: forest, meadow, steppe, rock. From the height of the ground and the wind it works out temperature and rain, then sorts every place into a biome by rules you write. A second rule turns the year: snow comes down in winter and leaves turn in autumn. Is it for me? ✅ You use Go Simulator and want weather and biomes . ✅ You want to set it up by writing a rules file : no programming needed. ✅ You are curious about the science behind it: the pages explain the model with pictures. Where to start Pick the line that sounds like you. If you… Read Time are new and want to see it work 🏴‍☠️ The quest : an island's weather and biomes, in 5 levels 45 min want to run its example Getting started 10 min want to know how the climate is worked out The model 15 min are looking up a parameter Rules reference — All the pages, in reading order The menu on the left (or the files in docs/ ) follows this order. Start Overview : this page The quest Getting started Understand The model How it works Reference Rules reference 🚧 Not done yet The climate does not change with time on its own: the climate rule works it out once (and again only when the world's ground changes, as the terrain's erosion rule makes it), and the seasons rule moves only the snow line and the foliage tint, not the temperature and precipitation fields. There is no weather yet (no single storms, no daily rain). The foliage tint is drawn only on materials marked as foliage; the made-up island in these pages has no vegetation, so its pictures show the snow but not the tint. The only example rules file, examples/mountain.yaml , works out the climate of a synthetic mountain without the seasons; the pages show the rest as rules to copy. Words you will meet Word What it means Terminal The window where you type commands: Terminal on macOS and Linux, PowerShell on Windows. Repository A project's folder of files, kept on GitHub. git clone <address> copies it to your computer. Plugin A small program that adds one ability to another: here, one kind of simulation each. Rules file A text file (YAML) that says which plugins to use, with which numbers, for how long: no programming needed. Field A grid of numbers laid over the world: the height of every spot, its temperature, its rain. Quest The tutorial of these docs: short levels, each ending with something that works and an achievement. The family Go Climate Simulator is one of a family of small projects that work together: Project What it does Go Renderer draws 3D scenes and flat interfaces Go UI buttons, panels and whole applications Go UI for Android Android apps that look like Android's own Go Sound sound and music Go Scene Builder 3D scenes from a flat map Go Simulator simulations that change a scene Go Terrain Simulator ground shaped by rivers Go Climate Simulator (this one) weather and biomes Go Flora Simulator forests that grow Go Urban Simulator towns that grow Go Motion Simulator a scene that moves Go for 3DS Go on the Nintendo 3DS ⚠️ All of them are educational experiments , written with an AI assistant and pending review by their author: good for learning and playing, not for production.

rules-reference.title: 📋 Rules of the climate plugin
rules-reference.text: 📋 Rules of the climate plugin Version 1.0.0, protocol 2. Yearly temperature and rain over a relief, the biome of every place, and the turning seasons. This reference is generated from what the plugin itself tells the host (the describe message), so it always matches the code. Parameters go under with: in a rules file; see Go Simulator's rules file reference . Rule What it does climate Works out temperature (fields: temperature, °C), rain (precipitation, mm a year) and biome (biome: index into the names of the "biomes" event, −1 for the sea) at the start, and again when the world's ground changes. seasons Turns the year: moves the snow line with the season's temperature and gives foliage the season's colour (environment). climate Works out temperature (fields: temperature, °C), rain (precipitation, mm a year) and biome (biome: index into the names of the "biomes" event, −1 for the sea) at the start, and again when the world's ground changes. Reads: fields elevation , drainage_area Writes: temperature , precipitation , biome Parameter Type Default Meaning relief text relief header (relieve.json with relieve.f32 next to it), km east and north; without it, the world's elevation origin list [east, north] of the world's origin: x = east − origin[0], z = origin[1] − north cell number 0.1 km: cell of the fields temperature map {sea_level: °C, lapse: °C per km, northward: °C per 10 km} rain map {wind_from: degrees, background: mm, orographic: mm, …} terrain map {river_area: km², river_slope, coast_reach: km, coast_low: m, coast_slope} biomes list rules: [{biome, when: {temperature, precipitation, height, slope: {min, max}, river, coast}}] regions list [{biome, ellipse: {centre, radii} | polygon, when}]: the world's own biomes layer text biomes.json: also save the biomes as a layer for Go Scene Builder (-layer biome=…), with their names, in km east and north seasons Turns the year: moves the snow line with the season's temperature and gives foliage the season's colour (environment). Reads: the environment Writes: environment Parameter Type Default Meaning year_length number 240 units of the stage's time a year lasts warmest number 0.3 when it is warmest, as a share of the year temperature map {sea_level: °C, lapse: °C per km, amplitude: °C above and below the mean} snow_at number 0 °C under which the ground is snowy snow_blend number 150 metres over which the snow fades in foliage list [{at: share of the year, color, amount}], interpolated around the year

the-model.title: 🌦️ The climate model
the-model.text: 🌦️ The climate model Where is it cold? Where does it rain? What grows there? The climate plugin answers these three questions for every place of a map, starting only from its relief, so that the answers always agree with each other and with the land: no snow at the beach, no rainforest in a rain shadow. The example island: mean temperature, yearly rain and the biomes that follow from them Colder on the mountain, wetter on the slope that faces the wind, and the biomes that follow. It works the climate out at the start and publishes three fields and an event: Output Content field temperature mean yearly temperature, °C field precipitation yearly rain and snow, mm field biome index into the names of the biomes event, −1 for the sea event biomes {"names": […]} , the biome of every index The grid has the cell given by cell (km), over the relief's extent; origin places the relief's kilometres east and north on the world ( x = east − origin[0] , z = origin[1] − north ). The relief is the relief file or, without one, the world's elevation , as the terrain plugin publishes it (put it first). On the world's ground the climate also takes the world's drainage_area when there is one (see below), and when that ground changes, because the terrain's erosion rule moved it, the climate is worked out again in the step after and published again. The maps and charts below are of a made-up island, 20 km by 15 km, with a ridge of about 2,550 metres in the east, run with the rules file in getting started . Temperature Air gets colder as you climb, by about 6.5 °C every kilometre. That is most of the story: temperature = sea_level − lapse × height_km + northward × (north − middle of the map) / 10 sea_level is the mean at sea level (°C), lapse the degrees lost per kilometre of height (6.5 is the standard atmosphere) and northward an optional gradient per 10 km (negative: colder to the north). Sea cells take the sea-level value. With sea_level: 12 and lapse: 6.5 , the coast is at 12 °C and the top of the ridge, about 2.5 km up, at about −4.5 °C. Rain Rain is the interesting part. Moist air blows in from one side; when it has to climb a mountain it cools and drops its water on the slope facing the wind, and by the time it comes down the other side it is dry: the rain shadow. The plugin follows that air across the map. A semi-Lagrangian moisture model carries it from where the wind comes ( wind_from , degrees clockwise from north): The relief the air feels is smoothed ( relief_scale , km), and the moisture is carried on a coarser grid ( calculation_cell , km), downwind, cell by cell: every cell takes the air of the cell upwind. Over land the air drops a share of its moisture every cell ( base ), more where it climbs ( rise , extra share per metre up per metre forward): orographic rain on the windward slopes. Over the sea it recovers a share of what it misses ( recharge ); over flat land, slowly ( evaporation ). Behind a ridge, the air is drier: the rain shadow. The rain of a place is background mm a year times the air's humidity there (1 = saturated: frontal rain) plus orographic mm times what the air dropped there, measured against the most exposed 3 % of the land. Both are smoothed by smoothing km. Without rain settings the defaults are neutral, for every world to set its own: the wind from the west, as the westerlies of the middle latitudes blow; 1,000 mm of background , about the world's mean (2.6 mm a day; Adler et al. 2003, the GPCP analysis); and 1,000 mm of orographic , which doubles the rain on the most exposed windward slopes, a moderate case of what mountain ranges show (Roe 2005). The same island with the wind turned round: everything else is the same, so the wet side and the rain shadow swap places. River valleys and coasts The area that drains through every land cell is followed downhill, from the highest cell to the lowest: each cell sends its water to the lowest of its eight neighbours. When the world has a drainage_area (the terrain's erosion rule publishes it, with hollows filled so all water reaches the sea), that one is used instead, so the climate's rivers are the terrain's: every cell of the climate's grid takes the largest area of the cells inside it, so a river one fine cell wide is not lost on a coarser grid. A cell is on a river valley when it drains more than river_area km² and is flatter than river_slope ; the valley floor is widened by two cells. A cell is on the coast when it is within coast_reach km of the sea, lower than coast_low metres and flatter than coast_slope . On the biome map below, riverside follows the island's three valleys down to the sea, and coast is the thin low rim where the land meets it. Biomes With heat and rain known, choosing the biome is a matter of rules, like a field guide: "colder than −2.5 °C: snow; steeper than 0.6: rock; otherwise, if it rains more than 1000 mm: forest…". Every land cell gets the first biome whose conditions hold, in the order written: biomes: - {biome: snow, when: {temperature: {max: -2.5}}} - {biome: rock, when: {slope: {min: 0.6}}} - {biome: riverside, when: {river: true}} - {biome: coast, when: {coast: true}} - {biome: forest, when: {temperature: {max: 11}, precipitation: {min: 1000}}} - {biome: steppe} # no conditions: everything left Conditions use Go Simulator's condition language over the facts of a cell: temperature , precipitation (mm), height (m), slope (rise over run), river_area (km² drained), and the yes/no facts river and coast . An unknown fact is an error. The island's table is the one above with a meadow rule ( precipitation: {min: 750} ) before steppe . Placing every place by its rain and temperature shows the table at work: each biome fills the box its conditions leave it. Regions Regions give areas of the map a biome of their own, over the table: an ellipse ( centre and radii , km east and north) or a polygon , with their own conditions. ragged (a share of the ellipse's size) makes the edge irregular, like a real forest's, with smooth value noise that is the same for the same place. regions: - {biome: old wood, ellipse: {centre: [3, 6], radii: [2, 1.5]}, ragged: 0.15, when: {height: {min: 150}}} Seasons The yearly mean is not the whole story when you watch a scene: snow comes down in winter and leaves turn in autumn. The seasons rule turns the year on any clock: the year lasts year_length units of the stage's time (months on a stepped clock, seconds on a real-time one), and warmest says when in the year it is warmest (a share: 0.35 is a little past a third). The temperature swings amplitude °C around the yearly mean, so the snow line, where the season's temperature falls below snow_at , climbs in summer and comes down in winter (with snow_blend metres of fade). Foliage takes the colour of the season from foliage stops ( {at, color, amount} ), interpolated around the year. It changes the environment ( snow and foliage_tint ); Go Renderer draws snow on surfaces that face up and tints materials marked as foliage. The snow biome and the season's snow are two different things: the biome is where the yearly mean is cold enough (a colour of the terrain, the same all year), the season's snow is drawn on top of everything above the snow line of the moment. Use cd ../go-simulator && go run ./cmd/simulate -rules climate.yaml -output results The flora plugin reads the fields from the world to grow vegetation. For Go Scene Builder , which colours the terrain and sows each biome's vegetation from a layer ( -layer biome=biomes.json ), give the rule a layer : - rule: climate with: {relief: relieve.json, origin: [3, 2], layer: biomes.json, …} It saves biomes.json and biomes.f32 once, at the start, next to the rules file (or where the path says). The grids Go Simulator saves in its snapshots will not do for this: their coordinates are the world's x and z, which move with origin , and the names of the biomes are not in them (they travel in the biomes event). The layer is in the relief's own kilometres east and north, like the scene builder's map and relief, and carries the names as labels ; the sea is −1, with no name. Getting started has a whole rules file and the way to the viewer. References Adler, R. F. et al. (2003). The version-2 Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP) monthly precipitation analysis (1979–present). Journal of Hydrometeorology 4. Roe, G. H. (2005). Orographic precipitation. Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences 33.

the-quest.title: The climate quest
the-quest.text: The climate quest Give an island its weather, one level at a time. Each level teaches one piece of the climate plugin and ends with the island coloured by its biomes : snow, rock, forest, meadow, steppe. The quest map: a road from START through 5 levels — Thermometer, Rainmaker, Naturalist, Gamekeeper and Almanac — to a final challenge, Forester We use the mountain island shaped in the terrain quest (any relief will do). It gets cold as it climbs, wet where the west wind meets it and dry behind it; rivers, cliffs and beaches find their own biomes; an old wood stands where the story puts it; and a year passes, with snow and autumn colours. Every level has the same shape: the idea (explained with something from everyday life), the rules , a checkpoint to know it works, and an optional bonus . Before you start You need Go 1.25 and GEOS ( sudo apt install libgeos-dev , brew install geos ). Clone the projects side by side and make a folder for the quest: git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-renderer git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-scene-builder git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-simulator git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-simulator-climate mkdir weather && cd weather Put the island's relief in it as island.json and island.f32 : from the terrain quest, the end snapshot results/island 200 elevation.json and .f32 , renamed. (Or write your own with the terrain quest's island/main.go .) Looking at the biomes The climate rule can save its biomes as a layer that Go Scene Builder colours the terrain with. Two small files, made once. empty.geojson , a map with nothing on it: {"type": "FeatureCollection", "properties": {"units": "km"}, "features": []} view.yaml , a colour for every biome: units: m chunk: 2 environment: {sun: [220, 35], water_level: 0} terrain: color: "#8a8674" biomes: snow: {color: "#eeeeea"} rock: {color: "#8a8674"} meadow: {color: "#a7b46a"} steppe: {color: "#c8b47a"} forest: {color: "#4f6b3a"} riverside: {color: "#6f9a5a"} coast: {color: "#d9cfa3"} old wood: {color: "#3b5230"} After every run: go run ../go-scene-builder/cmd/build-scene -map empty.geojson -relief island.json -layer biome=biomes.json -style view.yaml -out island.glb go run ../go-renderer/cmd/visor island.glb The pictures were taken with -zoom 0.75 -sun-azimuth 250 -sun-elevation 25 . Level 1 · The Thermometer Mission Pieces Time Colder as you climb, and snow on top climate , temperature , biome rules, layer 8 min The idea Climb a mountain and your ears pop and your hands get cold : the air cools about 6.5 °C for every kilometre up. That is the lapse rate . Start from the temperature at the sea and the height of every cell says how cold it is. Biomes are a list of rules read top to bottom, like a sorting hat : each cell gets the first biome whose conditions it meets. The last rule, with no conditions, catches everything left. Build it rules.yaml : plugins: - name: climate command: [go, run, .] directory: ../go-simulator-climate stages: - name: year clock: {unit: month, from: 0, to: 1, step: 1} snapshots: [1] snapshot_fields: [temperature, biome] rules: - rule: climate with: relief: island.json origin: [0, 0] layer: biomes.json temperature: {sea_level: 12, lapse: 6.5} biomes: - {biome: snow, when: {temperature: {max: 6}}} - {biome: meadow} go run ../go-simulator/cmd/simulate -rules rules.yaml -output results/ Checkpoint biomes.json and biomes.f32 appear next to the rules file, and results/ holds year 1 temperature and year 1 biome . On the island, a cap of snow above about a kilometre, and meadow everywhere else. Level 1: meadow all over the island, snow on its peak Bonus (optional): an ice age Achievement unlocked: Thermometer Learn more: The model · Rules Level 2 · The Rainmaker Mission Pieces Time Wet where the wind climbs, dry behind rain , precipitation in biome rules 8 min The idea Wind from the sea carries water. When it meets a mountain it climbs, cools and rains , like a sponge squeezed on the way up; past the top it comes down dry. So the side facing the wind is wet and green, and the other side, in its rain shadow , is dry. Build it In the climate rule, a west wind, and biomes by rain (millimetres a year): rain: {wind_from: 270, background: 450, orographic: 1400} biomes: - {biome: snow, when: {temperature: {max: 6}}} - {biome: forest, when: {precipitation: {min: 1500}}} - {biome: meadow, when: {precipitation: {min: 1250}}} - {biome: steppe} wind_from: 270 is a wind from the west; orographic is how much more rain the climb brings. Add precipitation to snapshot_fields to see the rain itself. Checkpoint A ring of dark forest on the high, wet slopes; meadow below; and the east side, behind the mountain, turns to tan steppe. Level 2: forest on the wet slopes, steppe on the dry east side Bonus (optional): an east wind Achievement unlocked: Rainmaker Level 3 · The Naturalist Mission Pieces Time Cliffs, riverbanks and beaches slope , river , coast , terrain 6 min The idea A naturalist knows that what grows depends on more than weather: nothing roots on a cliff , willows line the rivers , and the shore has its own plants. The plugin works out the slope, where water gathers into rivers and where the coast is, and the biome rules can ask for them. Order matters: the sorting hat takes the first rule that fits, so the special places come before the weather. Build it terrain: {river_area: 0.5, river_slope: 0.05} biomes: - {biome: snow, when: {temperature: {max: 6}}} - {biome: rock, when: {slope: {min: 0.6}}} - {biome: riverside, when: {river: true}} - {biome: coast, when: {coast: true}} - {biome: forest, when: {precipitation: {min: 1500}}} - {biome: meadow, when: {precipitation: {min: 1250}}} - {biome: steppe} Checkpoint Grey rock on the steepest cliffs of the coast, pale sand along the shore, and greener strips where the rivers run. Level 3: rock on the cliffs and sand along the shore Achievement unlocked: Naturalist Level 4 · The Gamekeeper Mission Pieces Time An old wood that the story puts there regions 5 min The idea Some places are not where the weather says, but where the story says: a royal hunting forest, an old wood with a name. A region is a stencil laid on the map: inside it, a biome of its own, where its conditions hold. ragged frays its edge so it does not look drawn with a compass. Build it After biomes , in the climate rule (the centre is in kilometres east and north): regions: - {biome: old wood, ellipse: {centre: [-1.5, -1], radii: [1.2, 0.8]}, ragged: 0.15, when: {height: {min: 100}}} Checkpoint A darker patch of old wood in the south-west, its edge frayed, never on the beach (it asks for 100 m at least). The biomes event in results/events.jsonl lists it among the names. Level 4: a darker old wood in the south-west of the island Achievement unlocked: Gamekeeper Level 5 · The Almanac Mission Pieces Time A year of seasons, live in the viewer seasons , a month clock, the live simulator 8 min The idea An almanac tells what each month brings. The seasons rule moves the snow line down in winter and up in summer, and tints the leaves through the year: fresh green in spring, dark in summer, orange in autumn. The renderer draws it on the scene as it runs. Build it A year of months, a quarter of a month every half second, and the seasons after the climate: clock: {unit: month, from: 0, to: 12, step: 0.25, pace: 0.5} snapshots: [0] rules: - rule: climate with: { … as before … } - rule: seasons with: year_length: 12 warmest: 0.55 temperature: {sea_level: 12, lapse: 6.5, amplitude: 8} snow_at: 0 snow_blend: 150 foliage: - {at: 0.25, color: "#9cc35a", amount: 0.15} - {at: 0.5, color: "#5d7a3c", amount: 0} - {at: 0.8, color: "#c8752f", amount: 0.6} - {at: 0.95, color: "#7a6e5f", amount: 0.6} Build the scene as before, then run it live : go run ../go-simulator/cmd/simulator -rules rules.yaml island.glb Checkpoint The year turns: in winter, snow down the mountain's shoulders; by summer, only the snow biome on the peak. -advance 26 starts in summer. Level 5 in winter: snow over the upper slopes Level 5 in summer: only the peak is white Bonus (optional): a harsher winter Achievement unlocked: Almanac Final challenge · Forester Fill the forest with trees : firs and oaks in the forest, oaks in the old wood and along the rivers, and watch them turn orange in autumn . Hint: Go Scene Builder sows models over a biome: terrain.biomes.<name>.decorate with the scatter recipe, and a model library. A part with material: {foliage: true} takes the seasons' tint.
